title: Zechariah 6:9–15
context: The LORD tells Zechariah to take silver and gold from returned exiles named Heldai, Tobijah, and Jedaiah, make crowns, and set them on Joshua the high priest. Zechariah announces “the man whose name is the Branch,” who will build the LORD’s temple, bear glory, and rule as a priest on his throne, with “the counsel of peace” between them both. The crowns are to be a memorial in the temple, and those far off will help build it, if the people diligently obey the LORD. The Branch is also named at 3:8, Jeremiah 23:5 and 33:15, and related hope appears in Haggai 2:23; these are read alongside the Davidic promise of 2 Samuel 7 without merging them. Readers identify the Branch in different ways, and many Christians see Christ in the joining of priest and king.

verses.text: The LORD’s word came to me, saying,
verses.arminianNotes:
The LORD’s word comes to Zechariah. The visions give way to a symbolic action.

Arminian readers see God now asking for a visible response from the community, so that the message of the visions is acted out in public.
verses.reformedNotes:
This section shifts from vision to command, linking the visions to Joshua and the temple.

Reformed readers see God directing his prophet in a sign. Shared ground: both traditions read this as God’s word guiding the community’s life after the return from exile.

verses.text: “Take of them of the captivity, even of Heldai, of Tobijah, and of Jedaiah; and come the same day, and go into the house of Josiah the son of Zephaniah, where they have come from Babylon.
verses.arminianNotes:
Zechariah is to take from the exiles Heldai, Tobijah, and Jedaiah, and go the same day to the house of Josiah son of Zephaniah. Returned exiles provide the gifts.

Arminian readers see the community participating in God’s purposes.
verses.reformedNotes:
The names in 6:14 differ (Helem and Hen for Heldai and Josiah). Readers explain this differently, and the text does not say.

Reformed readers see God using returnees. Shared ground: the names are held as the text gives them.

verses.text: Yes, take silver and gold, and make crowns, and set them on the head of Joshua the son of Jehozadak, the high priest;
verses.arminianNotes:
Zechariah is to make crowns of silver and gold and set them on Joshua son of Jehozadak, the high priest. A priest is crowned.

Arminian readers see a striking sign pointing beyond the usual roles.
verses.reformedNotes:
The plural “crowns” may mean a composite crown or more than one crown; only Joshua’s head is mentioned. Joshua is the high priest of Haggai 1:1 and Ezra 3:2 (there called Jeshua).

Reformed readers see the sign as significant. Shared ground: the act points forward.

verses.text: and speak to him, saying, ‘The LORD of Armies says, “Behold, the man whose name is the Branch! He will grow up out of his place; and he will build the LORD’s temple.
verses.arminianNotes:
Zechariah is to say, “Behold, the man whose name is the Branch!” who will grow up and build the LORD’s temple. The Branch is named.

Arminian readers see a promise of a coming builder.
verses.reformedNotes:
Zechariah 3:8 also mentions “my servant, the Branch,” and Jeremiah 23:5 and 33:15 speak of a Branch for David. Some read the Branch here as Zerubbabel; many Christians see Christ.

Reformed readers see the Davidic hope (2 Samuel 7) renewed. Shared ground: hope rests in God’s chosen king.

verses.text: He will build the LORD’s temple. He will bear the glory, and will sit and rule on his throne. He will be a priest on his throne. The counsel of peace will be between them both.
verses.arminianNotes:
The Branch will build the temple, bear glory, and rule on his throne as a priest, with “the counsel of peace” between them both. Priest and king are joined.

Arminian readers see harmony between royal and priestly roles.
verses.reformedNotes:
Whether “them both” means two persons or two offices in one person is debated. Some Christians connect this with Christ as priest and king (compare Psalm 110:4; Hebrews 7:17), though Hebrews does not cite this verse.

Reformed readers agree. Shared ground: both traditions read this with care.

verses.text: The crowns shall be to Helem, to Tobijah, to Jedaiah, and to Hen the son of Zephaniah, for a memorial in the LORD’s temple.
verses.arminianNotes:
The crowns will be a memorial in the LORD’s temple for Helem, Tobijah, Jedaiah, and Hen son of Zephaniah. The gifts are remembered.

Arminian readers see faithful giving honored before God.
verses.reformedNotes:
Helem and Hen may be other names for Heldai and Josiah (6:10), or “Hen” may describe the host’s kindness; readers differ.

Reformed readers see God remembering his people’s service. Shared ground: the memorial honors those who gave.

verses.text: Those who are far off shall come and build in the LORD’s temple; and you shall know that the LORD of Armies has sent me to you. This will happen, if you will diligently obey the LORD your God’s voice.” ’ ”
verses.arminianNotes:
Those far off will come and build the LORD’s temple, “if you will diligently obey the LORD your God’s voice.” Arminian readers see a real condition attached to the promise.

Compare the box at Deuteronomy 5:29.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see the command calling for obedience that God also works in his people.

Shared ground: both traditions read the condition as genuine covenant language, linking God’s promises with his people’s faithful response.
